title: Bamboo Paper Stamp Mill
premise: A master-apprentice relay at a bamboo paper workshop in southern Anhui. Master Bailu and apprentice Mili guard the bamboo papermaking screen; Mili and Aye look nearly alike but wear different sleeve covers; the green-bamboo pulp cart must be avoided after it wrecks; the pulp formula book, count memory, and temporal flashbacks run throughout. Human-readable context only; never fed to the SUT.

states.prime_papermaker: A forty-year-old papermaking master, blue-cloth headwrap, hemp apron soaked in pulp, hands blanched from soaking, wrists steady and precise.
states.scalded_with_cane: The same Bailu: forearm scalded by boiling pulp and wrapped in herbal cloth, leaning on a broken bamboo cane, one corner of the hemp apron charred.
states.died_in_mill: Bailu lies still with eyes closed on a wooden cot in the water-powered stamp mill, the hemp apron covering his chest.

states.young_apprentice: A fifteen-year-old apprentice girl in a plant-dyed apron, bamboo-strip bracelet on her wrist, fingertips often marked with white pulp.
states.adult_master: A woman master in her early twenties, still in the plant-dyed apron and bamboo-strip bracelet, upright posture, able to lift a full wet sheet in one motion.

states.intact: A fine bamboo papermaking screen, wires even and straight, old bamboo frame polished bright, surface coated with even white pulp.
states.screen_torn: The same bamboo papermaking screen with several wires snapped, frame cracked by floodwater, dried pulp crust jammed in the seams.

states.intact: A long narrow green-bamboo pulp cart, wooden trough holding softened bamboo fiber, sides lined with green bamboo-leaf sheaths, four small wooden wheels below.

segments.action: At dusk, Bailu rolls up the bamboo curtain door, enters the damp papermaking workshop, and lays the bamboo papermaking screen flat on the screen bed.
Five rows of wooden paper-drying clamp rods hang under the workshop beams; Bailu checks each row to see if the clamps will hold wet paper.
By the waterwheel two waterwheel wooden hammers fall in turn; Bailu listens to their rhythm pounding cooked bamboo.
Bailu dips the papermaking screen into the bamboo-pulp vat and gives a gentle shake, spreading a thin white pulp across the screen.
He lifts the first wet sheet onto the wall board, leaving tiny water beads on his fingertips.
Bailu unties the bamboo-sheath cord and opens the oil-paper-covered pulp formula book.
With pine-soot ink he records today's bamboo soak days, lime ratio, and paper batch number.
Bailu closes the formula book and leans the damp bamboo papermaking screen by the vat to drain.
At the bamboo-soaking pond in the morning, Bailu greets young apprentice Mili pushing the green-bamboo pulp cart.

segments.action: On a mountain-rain night months later, Bailu alone watches the vat in the papermaking workshop, the bamboo papermaking screen against his knee.
He opens the pulp formula book and finds wet pulp has crept from the desk corner; the oil-paper cover wrinkles, ink characters blur into gray-white blobs.

segments.action: Bailu scrapes pulp stains from the page edges with a bamboo slip and rewrites the still-readable ratios from memory.

segments.action: Through the long papermaking season, Bailu day after day dips screens, lifts sheets, and presses out water in the workshop.
When plum rains arrive, he moves the paper-drying clamp rods farther apart so wet sheets will not re-dampen and wrinkle.
As new bamboo comes to market, Bailu stands in the doorway watching bundles of green bamboo carried to the pond.
At high summer noon he fans heat from freshly lifted sheets with a cattail fan.
In endless autumn rain, lime smell and green-bamboo scent hang by the pulp vat.
On another New Year's Eve, Bailu alone keeps watch in the workshop until the waterwheel falls silent.
At dawn Bailu patrols along the bamboo-soaking pond; the green-bamboo pulp cart rests by the stone steps.
He crouches to check the pulp cart's four small wooden wheels, confirming none are jammed by bamboo fiber.
Bailu restacks scattered bamboo-strip bundles by the pond, leaving a path for the cart.
A cedar drying cart rolls in from the gallery direction, clamping half-dry paper sheets, but with no green bamboo-leaf sheaths and holding no bamboo fiber.
A mountain flood suddenly overruns the pond's stone steps; bamboo tubes and sheaths are swept up in muddy water.
Bailu snatches the bamboo papermaking screen from the workshop doorway, only to see the frame cracked by the current and the screen wires snapped.

segments.action: The green-bamboo pulp cart is shoved off the stone steps by the flood; bamboo fiber in the trough surges and spills.
The green-bamboo pulp cart smashes into the waterwheel base and breaks into slats; bamboo-leaf sheaths and one small wooden wheel drift into the muddy water.

segments.action: A bundle of green bamboo-leaf sheaths fallen from the green-bamboo pulp cart hangs by the wall; Bailu does not discard them for a long time.
Bailu takes one row from the five rows of paper-drying clamp rods under the beams and clamps a half-wet paper sample salvaged from the flood.
He places the remaining small wooden wheel from the green-bamboo pulp cart into a wooden box and covers it with old cloth.
Weeks later Bailu brings in an old bamboo craftsman to remeasure screen wires beside the workshop vat.

segments.action: The craftsman first offers a coarse screen mold frame for comparison—similar in shape, but sparse wires and no worn polish on the old bamboo frame.
Fine bamboo wires are worked into the tears one by one; the bamboo papermaking screen is restrung tight and the surface smooths again.

segments.action: A clay-jar handcart rolls up to the pond; the jar holds only clear water and lime—it is not the already wrecked and scrapped green-bamboo pulp cart.
The paper-shop bookkeeper steps beside Bailu to check paper batches; both wear blue-cloth headwraps, backs alike for a moment.
The bookkeeper points at the clay-jar handcart to arrange lime storage; Bailu keeps checking bamboo stock in the pond.
Suner from the next village carries bamboo sheaths to the pond; her light-brown apron from afar looks like young Mili's plant-dyed apron.
Suner tries to push a bamboo tube into the water, but Bailu shakes his head, noting her bamboo hairpin—she is not Mili after all.
At dusk years later, Bailu leans on a broken bamboo cane and slowly enters the half-collapsed abandoned water-powered stamp mill.
